core: Working definition of poverty: the state of lacking a usual or socially acceptable amount of money or material possessions — lacking the means to satisfy basic needs (attributed to Encyclopaedia Britannica)
Absolute vs relative poverty: fixed survival threshold vs the society's typical standard, with original examples (Ortiz family, Mei)

The measurement idea: Census poverty thresholds (vary by family size and composition, updated for inflation, a statistical yardstick) and the World Bank's international poverty line for extreme poverty; the honest note that measures are debated (official measure vs supplemental measures)
Who experiences poverty: patterns stated factually with attributed data only — feminization of poverty, unmarried mothers, the working poor, Census reporting by age groups
The causes debate: individual explanations vs structural explanations, each named descriptively, no policy position
The consequences: material hardship, chronic stress, and limited opportunity, each stated factually
The honest framing: poverty is a condition, not a character verdict — Britannica's warning that noneconomic connotations obscure the inability to provide for basic needs
supporting: Basic needs can be defined narrowly (survival) or broadly (the prevailing standard of living in the community) — the conceptual root of the absolute–relative distinction (Britannica)
The official U.S. measure counts pre-tax money income and excludes noncash benefits and tax credits, motivating supplemental measures (Census)
The Census Bureau publishes an annual poverty report and rates by major age groups (Poverty in the United States: 2024)
Structural causes in Britannica: cyclical poverty (business-cycle fluctuations, mass unemployment) and collective poverty (underdevelopment, unequal distribution of wealth)
OpenStax 9.2: women make up a disproportionate share of adults in poverty; about one in four unmarried mothers lives in poverty
OpenStax 9.2: the working poor — unskilled, low-paying jobs without benefits, often seasonal or temporary; millions work full time yet earn too little to support a family

Effects of poverty are harmful to both individuals and society (Britannica); lower income is associated with less education, less adequate health care, and less influence over everyday circumstances (OpenStax)
Collective poverty can be transmitted from generation to generation (Britannica)

claims.claim: Poverty is the state of one who lacks a usual or socially acceptable amount of money or material possessions; poverty is said to exist when people lack the means to satisfy their basic needs (Encyclopaedia Britannica's working definition).

Basic needs can be defined narrowly (as those necessary for survival) or broadly (as those reflecting the prevailing standard of living in the community); the broad reading reaches people whose nutrition, housing, and clothing keep them alive but fall short of the population's standard — the conceptual root of the absolute–relative distinction.

Absolute poverty is an economic condition in which a family or individual cannot afford basic necessities such as food and shelter, so that day-to-day survival is in jeopardy; the OpenStax 3e glossary calls it deprivation so severe that it puts day-to-day survival in jeopardy.
Relative poverty is not having the means to live the lifestyle of the average person in one's country — measured against the society's typical standard rather than against survival.

Following the Office of Management and Budget's Statistical Policy Directive 14, the U.S. Census Bureau determines poverty status by comparing a family's pre-tax money income against official thresholds that vary by family size and composition; a family below its threshold counts as in poverty. Thresholds are updated annually for inflation and do not vary geographically.

The Census Bureau states its thresholds are intended as a statistical yardstick, not as a complete description of what people and families need to live; the official measure uses money income before taxes and excludes capital gains, noncash benefits (e.g., food assistance, housing subsidies), and tax credits, which is why supplemental measures exist and why measurement is debated.
The Census Bureau publishes poverty data for the nation and by major age groups, including the annual report 'Poverty in the United States: 2024' and poverty threshold tables by family size.

The World Bank measures global poverty with an international poverty line for extreme poverty in low-income economies, expressed per person per day, with values converted using purchasing-power parities so they are comparable across countries; the global poverty lines were updated in June 2025.

Poverty is not distributed evenly: the 'feminization of poverty' is the worldwide pattern in which women, especially unmarried mothers, make up a disproportionate share of people in poverty; OpenStax reports about one in four unmarried mothers in the United States lives in poverty.

The working poor hold unskilled, low-paying jobs that rarely offer benefits and are often seasonal or temporary; even working full time, millions of the working poor earn incomes too meager to support a family.

Explanations of poverty divide into individual-focused accounts (choices, effort, skills; Britannica notes the long association of poverty with personal attributes such as an unwillingness to work and improvidence) and structural accounts (business-cycle fluctuations with mass unemployment, low wages that lag inflation, economic underdevelopment, and unequal distribution of wealth). The debate between them is live and contested.

Poverty has consequences: material hardship (struggling to pay rent, buy food, and afford basic medical care), harm to individuals and society, lower education and less adequate health care, less influence over the circumstances of daily life, and the possibility of being transmitted from one generation to the next.

Britannica warns that the noneconomic connotations poverty has acquired (poor health, low skills, an unwillingness to work, improvidence) tend to obscure the core fact of an inability to provide for one's basic needs — supporting the honest framing that poverty is a condition, not a character judgment.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How poverty should be defined and measured.
positions: A narrow standard: poverty is only the inability to meet needs necessary for survival (absolute poverty)
A broad standard: poverty includes falling short of the prevailing standard of living in one's community (relative poverty)

The official U.S. measure counts pre-tax money income and excludes noncash benefits and tax credits; the Census Bureau also publishes supplemental measures that include such resources, and the World Bank applies a different international line for global comparisons
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents all of these as different tools with different assumptions, states the honest note that measures are debated, and uses the Census Bureau's own 'statistical yardstick' language. No single measure is endorsed; no numbers are invented.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the causes of poverty lie in individuals or in social structure.
positions: Individual explanations: choices, effort, skills, spending habits
Structural explanations: job markets, wages, economic fluctuations, distribution of wealth
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes both families of explanation in one line each, attributes each to the sources (Britannica's cyclical/collective poverty and its noneconomic connotations; OpenStax's working-poor account), and takes no policy position — matching the descriptive teaching requirement for contested concepts.

Supports: the working definition of poverty as the state of lacking a usual or socially acceptable amount of money or material possessions, with poverty existing when people lack the means to satisfy basic needs; basic needs defined narrowly (survival) or broadly (the prevailing standard of living in the community) — the conceptual root of the absolute–relative distinction; the noneconomic connotations of the term (poor health, low skills, unwillingness to work, improvidence) and Britannica's warning that these obscure the inability to provide for basic needs; cyclical poverty (business-cycle fluctuations, mass unemployment in depressions and recessions) and collective poverty (underdevelopment, unequal distribution of wealth, generational transmission); and the general claim that the effects of poverty are harmful to both individuals and society. sourceRecords.title: How the Census Bureau Measures Poverty
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: the Census Bureau's procedure under OMB Statistical Policy Directive 14 — comparing family money income against official thresholds that vary by family size and composition, with a family below its threshold counted as in poverty; thresholds updated annually for inflation (CPI-U) and not varying geographically; 48 possible thresholds; the thresholds intended as a statistical yardstick, not a complete description of what families need to live; the official measure using pre-tax money income and excluding capital gains, noncash benefits (e.g., food assistance, housing subsidies), and tax credits; the existence of supplemental measures and the history of the official poverty measure. Facts synthesized; no source wording reproduced.
